qs.q: A 35-year-old patient is diagnosed with lymphoma. Biopsy reveals TdT-positive cells. The presentation overlaps significantly with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. What is the diagnosis?
qs.e: TdT (terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase) positivity is the hallmark of lymphoblastic lymphoma — it is negative in ALL other NHL types. Treated with ALL protocols.

qs.q: Which virus is associated with Adult T-cell Leukaemia/Lymphoma?
qs.e: Human T-lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1) is the causative agent of Adult T-cell Leukaemia/Lymphoma. This is a must-know association.

qs.q: Which BRAF mutation is present in >99% of Hairy Cell Leukaemia cases?
qs.e: BRAF V600E mutation is present in >99% of hairy cell leukaemia cases, making it both diagnostic and a therapeutic target (vemurafenib).

qs.q: A 62-year-old man presents with fatigue, fever and bruising. His full blood count shows WCC 40×10⁹/L with 25% circulating blasts, Hb 90 g/L and platelets 50×10⁹/L. Which investigation is required to definitively diagnose acute myeloid leukaemia?
o: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy
qs.e: Although the peripheral smear already shows circulating blasts, definitive diagnosis and subclassification of AML require bone marrow examination — combining morphology, cytochemistry, immunophenotyping, and cytogenetic/molecular analysis.
qs.s: Haematology Exam MCQs: Anemia, Leukemia, Coagulation Prep — Hematopathology III

qs.q: Which chromosomal translocation is pathognomonic of chronic myeloid leukaemia?
qs.e: This is the Philadelphia chromosome, producing the BCR-ABL fusion gene that defines CML. The other options are characteristic translocations of specific AML/ALL subtypes, not CML.
qs.s: Haematology Exam MCQs: Anemia, Leukemia, Coagulation Prep — Hematopathology III

qs.q: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) is characterized by accumulation of
qs.e: CLL is a clonal proliferation of functionally incompetent mature B cells (CD5+, CD23+, CD19+) that accumulate in blood, marrow, and lymph nodes.

qs.q: In acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), Auer rods are
o: Pathognomonic crystalline azurophilic inclusions in myeloblasts
qs.e: Auer rods are fused lysosomal granules forming needle-like inclusions specific to myeloid blasts; their presence confirms AML over ALL.

qs.q: AML M3 (acute promyelocytic leukaemia) is associated with
qs.e: t(15;17) creates PML-RARA fusion, blocking myeloid differentiation; ATRA (all-trans retinoic acid) induces differentiation and is curative.

es.q: A patient presents with gastric MALT lymphoma. Identify the specific infectious agent strongly associated with its pathogenesis. Name another infectious association for Adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma.
es.m: Gastric MALT lymphoma is strongly associated with H. pylori infection. Adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma is associated with HTLV-1.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Leukaemia is a cancer of blood-forming tissues, causing abnormal white blood cells. Diagnosis involves blood tests and bone marrow biopsy. Treatment aims to eliminate cancerous cells and restore normal blood counts, often with chemotherapy.

sections.p: Leukaemia is a malignant proliferation of blood cells, typically white blood cells, originating in the bone marrow. Diagnosis is suspected with abnormal blood counts and confirmed by bone marrow examination showing cancerous cells.
b: Characterised by uncontrolled growth of abnormal white blood cells.
These cells can infiltrate bone marrow, lymph nodes, spleen, and other organs.
Distinguished into acute or chronic, and lymphoid or myeloid lineages.

t.b: Screens for anaemia, high or low white blood cell counts, and low platelets. Abnormalities suggest leukaemia.
Microscopic examination of blood cells. Identifies abnormal cell morphology (e.g., blasts) and maturity. Confirms suspicion from CBC.
The definitive test to diagnose leukaemia, assess its type, and determine the percentage of cancerous cells. Essential for classification.

sections.p: Severity is primarily determined by the type of leukaemia (acute vs. chronic) and the presence of specific genetic mutations. Acute leukaemias are rapidly progressive and considered high-grade.
b: Acute leukaemias require immediate treatment due to rapid progression.
Chronic leukaemias progress more slowly and may be asymptomatic for years.
Specific genetic abnormalities influence prognosis and treatment intensity.

t.b: Classifies leukaemias based on morphology, immunophenotype, genetics, and clinical features. Provides prognostic information.
Uses factors like age, white blood cell count, and genetic markers to predict treatment response and survival. Guides intensity of therapy.

sections.p: While the exact cause is often unknown, risk factors include genetic predispositions, exposure to radiation or certain chemicals, and viral infections. Some genetic syndromes increase risk.
b: Ionising radiation exposure.
Exposure to certain chemotherapy drugs (e.g., alkylating agents).
Genetic syndromes like Down syndrome, Fanconi anaemia.
Viral infections (e.g., HTLV-1 for certain T-cell leukaemias).

t.b: Acquired or inherited mutations in DNA are fundamental to leukaemia development. These disrupt normal cell growth and differentiation.
Certain chemicals (e.g., benzene) and radiation can damage DNA, increasing leukaemia risk. This is a significant factor in occupational exposures.

sections.p: Symptoms are often non-specific and related to bone marrow failure: anaemia causing fatigue, thrombocytopenia causing bruising/bleeding, and neutropenia causing infections. Enlarged lymph nodes or spleen may be present.
b: Fatigue, pallor, shortness of breath (anaemia).
Easy bruising, petechiae, nosebleeds, prolonged bleeding (thrombocytopenia).
Recurrent or persistent infections (neutropenia).
Bone pain, fevers, weight loss, night sweats.

t.b: Result from the replacement of normal blood-forming cells by leukaemic cells. This leads to deficiencies in red cells, platelets, and normal white cells.
Leukaemic cells can infiltrate organs like the liver, spleen, lymph nodes, and central nervous system, causing organ-specific symptoms.

sections.p: A combination of blood tests, bone marrow examination, and imaging is used. Genetic and molecular testing is crucial for accurate classification and prognosis.
b: Blood counts and morphology are initial steps.
Bone marrow biopsy is essential for diagnosis.
Cytogenetics and molecular studies refine diagnosis and guide therapy.

t.b: Identifies cell surface markers to determine the lineage (lymphoid/myeloid) and subtype of leukaemic cells. Crucial for precise classification.
Detects chromosomal abnormalities (translocations, deletions) in leukaemic cells. Many leukaemias have characteristic chromosomal changes that affect prognosis.
Detects specific gene mutations or fusion genes (e.g., BCR-ABL). Highly sensitive for identifying leukaemic clones and monitoring minimal residual disease.
Used to assess the extent of leukaemic infiltration in organs (lymph nodes, spleen, CNS, bone). Helps stage disease and detect complications.

sections.p: Immediate referral is needed for suspected acute leukaemia. Complications include severe infections due to neutropenia, life-threatening bleeding from thrombocytopenia, tumour lysis syndrome, and central nervous system involvement.
b: Severe, uncontrolled bleeding.
High fever with neutropenia.
Neurological symptoms (headache, confusion, seizures).
Tumour lysis syndrome (rapid breakdown of leukaemic cells).

t.b: Neutropenia significantly increases susceptibility to bacterial, fungal, and viral infections, which can be rapidly fatal.
Severe thrombocytopenia can lead to spontaneous or uncontrollable haemorrhage, particularly in the gastrointestinal tract or brain.
Occurs when large numbers of leukaemic cells are rapidly destroyed, releasing intracellular contents (potassium, phosphate, uric acid) into the blood, causing metabolic derangement and kidney injury.

sections.p: Treatment depends on leukaemia type and risk factors, typically involving chemotherapy. Targeted therapies and stem cell transplantation may be used for specific types or refractory disease. Supportive care is vital.
b: Chemotherapy is the mainstay for most leukaemias.
Targeted therapies exploit specific genetic abnormalities.
Stem cell transplant offers a cure for some.
Supportive care includes transfusions and infection management.

t.b: Uses cytotoxic drugs to kill leukaemic cells. Drug classes include anthracyclines, antimetabolites, and alkylating agents. Chosen based on leukaemia subtype and patient factors.
Drugs that specifically target molecular pathways or proteins crucial for leukaemic cell survival (e.g., tyrosine kinase inhibitors for CML).

Includes blood product transfusions (red cells, platelets), antibiotics for infections, and management of metabolic complications like TLS. Essential to manage side effects and prevent life-threatening events.

sections.p: Regular monitoring for relapse is essential. Prevention focuses on avoiding known risk factors like radiation and certain chemical exposures, though many cases are sporadic.
b: Long-term surveillance for minimal residual disease.
Monitoring for treatment side effects and secondary malignancies.
Genetic counselling for families with hereditary predispositions.

t.b: Highly sensitive tests (e.g., PCR, flow cytometry) to detect leukaemic cells below the level of microscopic detection. Guides treatment decisions and predicts relapse risk.
Minimising exposure to ionising radiation and known carcinogenic chemicals can reduce risk. Avoiding smoking is also important.

sections.p: Leukaemia can be mistaken for other causes of anaemia, infection, or enlarged lymph nodes. Conditions like lymphoma, myelodysplastic syndromes, and aplastic anaemia share some features.
b: Lymphoma.
Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS).
Aplastic anaemia.
Infectious mononucleosis.
Other causes of cytopenias.

t.b: Both are cancers of lymphocytes, but lymphoma typically arises in lymph nodes or lymphoid tissue, while leukaemia arises in bone marrow.
Disorders of ineffective blood cell production in the bone marrow, often with dysplasia. Can transform into acute myeloid leukaemia.

sections.p: A normal white blood cell count does not exclude leukaemia, especially in chronic forms or when leukaemic cells are mature. Early stages can present with subtle symptoms.
b: Normal CBC in early chronic leukaemia.
Leukaemic cells may have normal morphology.
Infections can mimic leukaemic symptoms.
Platelet counts can be normal initially.

t.b: Some leukaemic cells can appear morphologically normal or mature, especially in chronic leukaemias, making diagnosis challenging without further tests.
Not all leukaemias present with a high blast count; chronic leukaemias may have predominantly mature or slightly abnormal cells.

whenToSeekHelp: Persistent bone pain or unexplained fevers.
Neurological symptoms like severe headache or confusion.

faq.a: Yes, particularly certain types of acute leukaemia and chronic myeloid leukaemia, especially with modern treatments like targeted therapy and stem cell transplantation.
No, leukaemia is not contagious and cannot be spread from person to person.

faq.q: What is the difference between leukaemia and lymphoma?
faq.a: Leukaemia originates in the bone marrow and affects blood cells circulating in the body, while lymphoma originates in lymph nodes or lymphoid tissues.
